chapter_title: ROS Parameters and the Parameter Server
chapter_summary:
As your ROS application grows, you will have many configuration values that need to be shared across nodes: the robot's name, the sensor read frequency, the PID controller gains, the simulation mode, the map file path, and so on. Hardcoding these values in your source code is a bad practice because it requires recompilation every time you change a setting. ROS provides the **Parameter Server** — a shared, dictionary-like key-value store that allows nodes to read and write configuration values at runtime.

The Parameter Server is created automatically when you run `roscore`. It is accessible to all nodes on the ROS network. Parameters are stored as typed values: integers, floats, booleans, strings, lists, and dictionaries. Each parameter has a unique name (like a filesystem path) such as `/robot_name`, `/sensor_frequency`, or `/robot1/pid_gains/kp`.

**Setting and getting parameters from the command line:**

```bash
# Set a parameter
rosparam set /robot_name "my_robot"
rosparam set /sensor_frequency 40
rosparam set /simulation_mode false

# Get a parameter
rosparam get /robot_name
# Output: my_robot

# List all parameters
rosparam list

# Delete a parameter
rosparam delete /robot_name

# Dump all parameters to a YAML file
rosparam dump params.yaml

# Load parameters from a YAML file
rosparam load params.yaml
```

YAML is the standard format for parameter files. A YAML file for robot configuration might look like:

```yaml
robot_name: "turtlebot_01"
simulation_mode: false
sensor_frequency: 40

pid_gains:
  kp: 2.0
  ki: 0.1
  kd: 0.5

waypoints:
  - [0.0, 0.0]
  - [1.0, 2.0]
  - [3.0, 1.0]
```

**Accessing parameters from Python nodes:**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rospy.init_node('param_reader')
    
    # Get parameters with default values
    robot_name = rospy.get_param('/robot_name', 'default_robot')
    sensor_freq = rospy.get_param('/sensor_frequency', 10)
    simulation = rospy.get_param('/simulation_mode', True)
    
    # Get nested parameters
    kp = rospy.get_param('/pid_gains/kp', 1.0)
    
    rospy.loginfo("Robot: %s, Freq: %d Hz, Sim: %s, Kp: %.2f",
                  robot_name, sensor_freq, simulation, kp)
    
    # Set a parameter
    rospy.set_param('/status', 'running')
```

**Accessing parameters from C++ nodes:**

```cpp
#include <ros/ros.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    ros::init(argc, argv, "param_reader");
    ros::NodeHandle nh;
    
    std::string robot_name;
    int sensor_freq;
    bool simulation;
    double kp;
    
    // Get parameters with default values
    nh.param<std::string>("/robot_name", robot_name, "default_robot");
    nh.param<int>("/sensor_frequency", sensor_freq, 10);
    nh.param<bool>("/simulation_mode", simulation, true);
    nh.param<double>("/pid_gains/kp", kp, 1.0);
    
    ROS_INFO("Robot: %s, Freq: %d Hz, Sim: %d, Kp: %.2f",
             robot_name.c_str(), sensor_freq, simulation, kp);
    
    // Set a parameter
    nh.setParam("/status", "running");
    
    return 0;
}
```

**Private vs. global parameters:**

Parameters can be prefixed with the node's name to make them **private** to that node:

```python
# In a node named 'motor_controller'
# This creates a parameter at /motor_controller/max_speed
rospy.get_param('~max_speed', 1.0)
```

The tilde `~` indicates a private parameter. Private parameters are useful for node-specific settings that should not conflict with other nodes. For example, two motor controller nodes (`/left_motor` and `/right_motor`) can each have their own `~max_speed` parameter without conflict.

Global parameters (with a leading `/`) are shared across all nodes. They are useful for system-wide settings like the robot name or simulation mode.

**Parameter best practices:**
- Use parameters for any value that might change between deployments or experiments.
- Use YAML files to store parameter sets for different configurations (e.g., `simulation_params.yaml`, `real_robot_params.yaml`).
- Use private parameters for node-specific settings to avoid naming conflicts.
- Document all parameters in your package's README or documentation.
- Validate parameter values when reading them (e.g., check that a frequency is positive).

narration.text: In this chapter we learn a simple but powerful idea: keep configuration out of source code and in the Parameter Server. The Parameter Server is a shared key-value store started by the core ROS system. It holds typed values like integers, floats, booleans, strings, lists, and dictionaries so nodes can read and write configuration at runtime. That means you can tune sensor rates, controller gains, or a robot name without rebuilding a node. You'll see how to set parameters from the command line, load and dump YAML files, and read values from Python and C++ nodes with sensible defaults. We'll also contrast global parameters — accessible to every node — with private parameters, which live under a node's namespace and prevent naming conflicts when many nodes of the same type run. Throughout the lesson you'll practice crafting a YAML parameter file, loading it, and writing small nodes that read nested values. By the end, you'll understand when to use private parameters, how to validate values, and how to reload configuration during an experiment without a full rebuild. What configuration will you move out of code first?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives focus your practice and make evaluation concrete. First, you will use the ROS Parameter Server to store and retrieve configuration values so a running node can adapt without recompilation. For example, you'll set a sensor frequency or robot name from the command line and see the node read it. Second, you'll learn to set parameters from three sources: the rosparam command line, from inside nodes, and by loading YAML files. Practically, this means building a YAML file with nested dictionaries and lists and then loading it to test different deployments. Third, you'll understand the difference between private, node-scoped parameters and global parameters. You'll see why a tilde prefix creates node-local settings that avoid conflicts when multiple identical nodes run. Finally, you will work with parameter types: strings, integers, floats, booleans, and lists, and learn to supply default values and simple validation. Each objective maps to hands-on tasks in the activity so you can verify your competency with real nodes and files.

screens.title: What is the Parameter Server?
screens.subtitle: A shared, typed dictionary for runtime configuration

narration.text: The Parameter Server is a central, shared key-value store used by ROS to keep configuration separate from code. It starts automatically when the system core runs and is accessible to every node on the ROS network. Parameters in this store are typed — you can store integers, floats, booleans, strings, lists, and dictionaries — and each parameter is addressed with a name that looks like a filesystem path, for example a slash-prefixed robot name or nested keys for PID gains. This structure makes it natural to keep related values grouped under a common namespace. A concrete example: store a PID configuration under /pid_gains/kp so any controller can look up the proportional gain without hardcoding it. A common misconception is thinking the Parameter Server replaces persistent storage: it is intended for runtime configuration and is not a full database; parameters are available while the ROS master runs and are best stored in YAML files for reproducibility. Key takeaway: use the Parameter Server to separate configuration from compiled code, and keep parameter names organized with sensible namespaces so your nodes can find the values they expect.

screens.title: Using rosparam on the command line
screens.subtitle: Set, get, list, delete, dump and load parameters

narration.text: The rosparam command-line tools are essential for quick experiments and checks. Use rosparam set to write a key and value to the Parameter Server, for example setting a robot name or a sensor frequency while the system runs. Use rosparam get to read a stored value and verify the type. rosparam list shows all parameter names currently available, which is handy to inspect namespaces and private parameters after launching nodes. If a parameter is wrong or no longer needed, rosparam delete removes it. Two useful commands help with reproducibility: rosparam dump saves the current parameter tree to a YAML file, and rosparam load applies a YAML file into the server. A concrete workflow: start roscore, launch your nodes, tweak parameters with rosparam set, then use rosparam dump to create a snapshot before an experiment. A common misconception is thinking rosparam load replaces all values; it merges the YAML contents into the server, so be deliberate about key names. Key takeaway: rosparam is your live experiment control for parameters and a quick way to sanity-check values during tests. Using rosparam on the command line means use rosparam set/get/list/delete for live edits and rosparam dump/load to persist or restore parameter snapshots.. In practical terms, set, get, list, delete, dump and load parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › rosparam CLI
Command cheatsheet
# Set a parameter
rosparam set /robot_name "my_robot"
rosparam set /sensor_frequency 40
rosparam set /simulation_mode false

# Get a parameter
rosparam get /robot_name

# List parameters
rosparam list

# Delete a parameter
rosparam delete /robot_name

# Dump and load
rosparam dump params.yaml
rosparam load params.yaml
Use these commands during an experiment for quick tuning. Remember that dump captures the server state and load merges values into the server.
Practical example
Suppose a sensor is noisy at 40 Hz. Use rosparam set /sensor_frequency 20 while testing; the node reading that parameter can adapt on its next check. After tuning, use rosparam dump to save the tuned configuration.
Common misconception
rosparam load will overwrite everything. In fact it merges keys; keys present in the YAML will be set or updated, others remain unchanged.
Pro tip
Dump a params.yaml before a long run so you can restore the exact configuration if you need to repeat the experiment.

screens.title: YAML for parameter files
screens.subtitle: Author nested, typed parameters for reproducible experiments

narration.text: YAML is the standard format for parameter files in ROS because it's human-readable and supports nested structures and lists. A typical robot configuration file includes scalars and nested dictionaries for related settings like PID gains and waypoints. For example, declare robot_name as a string, simulation_mode as a boolean, sensor_frequency as an integer, a pid_gains mapping with numeric gains, and waypoints as a list of coordinate pairs. When you load this file with rosparam load, the server stores each entry under its top-level names and nested paths, which nodes can retrieve by the same names. A common pitfall is using tabs or incorrect indentation in YAML; always use spaces and test loading your file with rosparam load to confirm parsing. Another practical point: maintain multiple YAML files for different environments, for example simulation and real_robot, and keep them in your package so experiments are reproducible. Key takeaway: YAML files provide a stable, versionable source of parameter truth for your experiments and should be the canonical record of configuration you share with teammates. YAML for parameter files means keep parameter definitions in yaml for clarity, nesting, lists, and reproducibility across experiments.. In practical terms, author nested, typed parameters for reproducible experiments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Real-world tip

screens.title: Reading parameters in Python with rospy
screens.subtitle: Use get_param with defaults, read nested entries, and set parameters programmatically

narration.text: Python's rospy offers straightforward accessors for parameters. Use rospy. get_param with a key and an optional default value so your node has a safe fallback when a parameter is missing. In practice, call rospy. init_node early, then read values like robot_name, sensor_frequency, and nested keys such as pid_gains/kp. If a parameter must be written back into the server, use rospy. set_param. A concrete example: write a small param_reader node that logs the robot name and kp; use sensible defaults to avoid crashes if someone forgets to load a YAML file. A common misconception is assuming get_param will always return the correct type; the server stores typed values, but you should still validate ranges after reading (check frequency is positive, gains are within expected bounds). Finally, when writing a long-running node that may adapt to changes, periodically re-read parameters or implement a callback-based reconfiguration so the node responds to updated values without a restart. This practice keeps your experiments flexible and safe. Reading parameters in Python with rospy means use rospy.get_param with defaults and rospy.set_param to read and update typed parameters; validate values after reading.. In practical terms, use get_param with defaults, read nested entries, and set parameters programmatically. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Python Access
param_reader.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('param_reader')

  # Get parameters with defaults
  robot_name = rospy.get_param('/robot_name', 'default_robot')
  sensor_freq = rospy.get_param('/sensor_frequency', 10)
  simulation = rospy.get_param('/simulation_mode', True)
  kp = rospy.get_param('/pid_gains/kp', 1.0)

  rospy.loginfo("Robot: %s, Freq: %d Hz, Sim: %s, Kp: %.2f",
                robot_name, sensor_freq, simulation, kp)

  # Set a status parameter
  rospy.set_param('/status', 'running')
This example shows defaults to avoid crashes when parameters are missing. Always perform validation after reading numeric values.
Example use
Start your node, then change a parameter from the CLI. If your node re-reads the value, it can adapt without restart.
Misconception
Don't rely on type coercion. Treat values as typed and validate ranges explicitly to avoid unexpected behavior.
Check your understanding
How would you make your node respond to updated parameter values without restarting? Consider a re-check loop or a dynamic reconfigure approach.

screens.title: Reading parameters in C++ with NodeHandle
screens.subtitle: Use nh.param templates and setParam to access typed values

narration.text: C++ nodes use the NodeHandle A P I to access parameters with template methods that provide type-safety and defaults. Use nh. param with a template type to read a value and specify a default if the parameter is missing. For nested parameters like pid_gains/kp, request the correct numeric type and then validate it. To write parameters, call nh. setParam. A concrete example is a param_reader node that reads a string robot name, an integer sensor frequency, a boolean simulation flag, and a double kp. Logging these values helps confirm parity with the Python reader. A common contrast is that Python get_param is dynamically typed and returns Python types, whereas C++'s template methods enforce the expected type at compile time. This helps catch type mismatches early, but you still must validate numeric ranges and presence semantics at runtime. Key takeaway: use nh. param with sensible defaults and check values before using them in control loops to avoid unsafe behavior. Reading parameters in C++ with NodeHandle means use nh.param templates with defaults for type-safe parameter access and nh.setparam to write values back to the server.. In practical terms, use nh.param templates and setparam to access typed values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › C++ Access
param_reader.cpp
#include <ros/ros.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "param_reader");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;

  std::string robot_name;
  int sensor_freq;
  bool simulation;
  double kp;

  nh.param("/robot_name", robot_name, "default_robot");
  nh.param("/sensor_frequency", sensor_freq, 10);
  nh.param("/simulation_mode", simulation, true);
  nh.param("/pid_gains/kp", kp, 1.0);

  ROS_INFO("Robot: %s, Freq: %d Hz, Sim: %d, Kp: %.2f",
           robot_name.c_str(), sensor_freq, simulation, kp);

  nh.setParam("/status", "running");
  return 0;
}
C++ templates provide compile-time type guidance. Validate numeric ranges after reading to guard controllers and loops.
Practical check
Build and run this node alongside the Python reader to confirm both languages see the same values from your YAML file.
Contrast
Python is flexible but dynamic; C++ enforces types. Use both as checks — a wrong type in YAML can surface differently in each language.
Takeaway
Use consistent parameter names and types across languages to avoid integration issues between nodes.

screens.title: Private vs Global parameters
screens.subtitle: Use node-scoped parameters to avoid naming collisions

narration.text: Private parameters live under a node's namespace and are created by using a tilde prefix. This means a node named motor_controller that requests ~max_speed will result in a parameter stored as /motor_controller/max_speed. Global parameters start with a leading slash and are visible to every node. Use global parameters for system-wide settings like robot_name or simulation_mode. The benefit of private parameters is avoiding collisions — when you run two similar nodes such as left_controller and right_controller, each can have its own ~max_speed without interfering. A common misconception is believing private parameters are inaccessible from other nodes; they are accessible if you know the full namespace path, but by convention they are treated as node-local. Practical advice: prefer private parameters for component-level tuning and global parameters for environment or scenario settings. Key takeaway: choose scoping deliberately to prevent accidental overrides while keeping shared settings available across the system. Private vs Global parameters means private parameters (tilde) create node-local keys; global parameters (leading slash) create system-wide keys — use both intentionally to manage conflicts.. In practical terms, use node-scoped parameters to avoid naming collisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: Private parameters (tilde) create node-local keys; global parameters (leading slash) create system-wide keys — use both intentionally to manage conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Private vs Global
Global parameters
Use a leading slash, e.g. /robot_name. These values are shared across all nodes and useful for environment-wide settings. They are simple to access from any node without resolving a namespace.
Example
/robot_name = "turtlebot_01" used by navigation, logging, and UI nodes.
Private parameters
Use the tilde form ~max_speed when reading; it is stored under the node namespace, preventing conflicts when multiple instances run.
Example
Two motor controllers can each have ~max_speed and be launched under different node names, resulting in /left_motor/max_speed and /right_motor/max_speed.
Misconception
Private parameters are secret; in reality they are simply namespaced. Any node can read them if given the full path, but the convention is to treat them as local.
Takeaway
Use private parameters for node-specific tuning and global parameters for environment configuration to keep behavior predictable and collision-free.

screens.title: Parameter best practices
screens.subtitle: YAML sets, validation, documentation, and naming conventions

narration.text: Good parameter hygiene keeps experiments reproducible and safe. First, store parameter sets in YAML files per deployment: simulation_params. yaml and real_robot_params. yaml. Treat YAML as the canonical source of truth, and use rosparam load to apply configurations. Second, validate values when reading them: check that a frequency is positive and that PID gains are within a safe range before using them in a control loop. Third, use private parameters for node-level tuning and global parameters for shared environment values, and keep a consistent naming convention — for example, use lower_snake_case and group related keys under a common namespace. Fourth, document every parameter in your README including expected type, default, and purpose so teammates can run experiments without guesswork. A common oversight is neglecting to re-dump parameters after tuning; always save tuned sets to YAML so you can reproduce an experiment. Key takeaway: plan parameter structure and validation early so your code stays robust across deployments. Parameter best practices means use yaml for versioned sets, validate at read time, use private namespacing to avoid conflicts, and document parameters for reproducibility.. In practical terms, yaml sets, validation, documentation, and naming conventions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

YAML sets
Keep separate files per environment and version them in your package for repeatable experiments.
Validation
After reading, ensure numeric ranges are safe. A negative frequency is a common misconfiguration and should be rejected.

Group related keys and use private parameters for node-specific values to avoid clashes when multiple instances run.

screens.title: Build the robot_config.yaml and test
screens.subtitle: Create a YAML, load it, and validate parameters in nodes

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties together everything you've learned. Create a file named robot_config. yaml that includes robot_name, max_speed, sensor_frequency, pid_gains with kp, ki, kd, and a list of waypoints. Next, start roscore and run rosparam load robot_config. yaml to place these values on the server. As a test, write a Python node param_reader dot P Y file that reads each field with defaults and logs them, and a C++ node param_reader. cpp that does the same. Validate the numeric fields in each node: check that sensor_frequency is positive and max_speed is within an expected range. Run both nodes and compare their logs to verify both languages parse nested structures and lists correctly. Finally, change max_speed in the YAML file, run rosparam load again, and observe that your nodes can pick up the updated value if they re-check parameters or implement a re-read loop. This practice shows how configuration changes can be applied quickly without recompiling, giving you rapid iteration during tests. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: YAML parsing, type mismatches, and scoping errors

narration.text: When working with parameters, several recurrent mistakes slow people down. First, YAML parsing errors caused by tabs or misindentation are frequent; always use spaces and test the file with rosparam load on a clean roscore to confirm it parses. Second, type mismatches happen when a YAML value's type doesn't match the node's expectation; C++ will use the template type and Python will return the stored type, so keep consistent types across files and code. Third, scoping errors occur when a node looks for a private parameter but the YAML used global names; ensure you either load parameters under the intended namespace or use fully qualified names. Fourth, forgetting to validate values can lead to unsafe behavior; check ranges and set safe defaults. Practical debugging steps: use rosparam list to inspect namespaces, rosparam get to verify values, and add clear log messages in your nodes that print parameter values at startup. Key takeaway: verify YAML structure, types, and namespaces early, and add runtime validation so misconfigurations fail gracefully. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these three ideas in mind as you work with ROS parameters. First, the Parameter Server is a shared, typed key-value store that keeps configuration separate from code and allows runtime changes. Second, use rosparam and YAML files to manage parameter sets: rosparam set/get/list/delete plus dump and load let you edit and persist configurations, while YAML files serve as versionable records. Third, plan parameter scoping deliberately: use private parameters for node-specific tuning and global parameters for system-wide flags; always validate types and ranges after reading. These core concepts will guide your decisions about where configuration lives, how it is shared, and how to keep experiments reproducible and safe. narration.text: Before you run an experiment, run these three checks. First, confirm your YAML loads cleanly with rosparam load and inspect the server with rosparam list and get. Third, validate numeric values and set safe defaults so controllers do not act on invalid inputs. These small checks save time and avoid dangerous behavior on real robots.
